newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices recover in thin market.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices recover in thin market.

text.p: World oil prices drifted lower for much of the day in very thin volume but recovered later to trade in a narrow range with little scope for sharp moves either way, brokers said.

International benchmark Brent crude from the North Sea for January delivery was at 1548 GMT trading seven cents higher at $22.67 a barrel, having earlier drifted to an intra-day low of $22.49 a barrel.

Traders at the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) said volume was very thin in the absence of any direction from the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), which has been closed since Thursday for Thanksgiving.

The volume traded on the front month contract by 1526 GMT was 9,851 lots, compared to a daily average of 40,500 so far this month. The IPE will close early at 1730 GMT on Friday, reflecting the NYMEX holiday.

Prices have weakened slightly since Thursday's news that Turkey expects Iraqi crude to start flowing through the trans-Turkey oil pipeline by December 15. It will then be exported from the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) agreed on Thursday to roll over its current output ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) to support robust oil prices.

The ceiling takes into account 800,000 bpd of Iraqi crude which is expected to flow on implementation of the U.N. "oil-for-food" plan allowing crude exports worth $2.0 billion over six months to allow Iraq to buy food and medicines.
"It's all very quiet and we are just waiting to see what happens when Iraqi oil returns," a trader for an oil company said.

The absence of Iraqi crude exports, which have been under embargo since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, was partly responsible for prices rising to their highest level in five years in October.

With crude and heating oil inventories low, the market had expected Iraqi exports to start in September under the U.N. deal. But Iraqi military activity in northern Iraq led to U.S. retaliatory action and postponement of the limited sales agreement.

The U.N. Sanctions Committee has approved the December pricing formula submitted by Iraq. Oil industry sources said Iraqi state oil firm SOMO had priced its Kirkuk Blend crude for Westbound sales at a $1.55 discount to Dated (physical) Brent.
Physical Brent was valued at just under $23 a barrel on Friday afternoon.
